description: We are a Bahrain-based team skilled in AI, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Data Science, Python, Robotics, and Hardware. Our space-related research experience includes designing experiments, testing prototypes, and analyzing data. For Earth Systems Trend Detective, we aim to turn NASA data into clear environmental insights. We welcome skills in statistics, GIS, web development, and UI/UX. Join us to learn, experiment, and innovate together!
summary:
ALDANA developed an interactive web dashboard to explore 25 years of NASA satellite observations of Bahrain’s land surface temperature, covering 2001–2025. Using the MODIS Terra MOD11A2 dataset, we analyzed daytime and nighttime temperatures and their matched difference through quality filtering, geospatial processing, and monthly time-series analysis.

Our solution addresses the **Be an Earth Systems Trend Detective** challenge by showing what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the trends have statistical support. We used linear regression, confidence intervals adjusted approximately for temporal dependence, and false-discovery-rate control across map pixels.

The analysis identified a supported nighttime surface-temperature increase of approximately **1.09°C per decade**, while the full-period daytime trend was statistically inconclusive. We communicate limitations, including satellite observation-time changes and the distinction between surface and air temperature.

By translating complex satellite records into accessible maps and visualizations, ALDANA helps students and researchers investigate environmental change in Bahrain and identify priorities for further study and field measurements.
details:
ALDANA: Bahrain Surface Temperature Trends, 2001–2025

ALDANA is an interactive web dashboard that helps users investigate changes in Bahrain’s land surface temperature using 25 years of NASA satellite observations. Developed for the Be an Earth Systems Trend Detective challenge, it addresses four questions: What is changing? Where is it changing? How much is it changing? How strong is the statistical evidence?

How it works

We used NASA’s MODIS/Terra MOD11A2 Version 6.1 dataset, which provides eight-day land surface temperature composites at approximately one-kilometer spatial resolution. Our analysis covers 1,148 composites from 2001–2025, organized into 300 monthly time steps.

The processing workflow filters observations using quality indicators, converts valid temperature values into degrees Celsius, applies geographic boundaries, and generates regional and pixel-level analyses. We examined daytime temperature, nighttime temperature, and their difference using matched valid observations.

To distinguish long-term changes from the average seasonal cycle, we calculated monthly anomalies relative to a 2001–2020 baseline. We estimated linear trends, calculated confidence intervals with an approximate AR(1) adjustment for temporal dependence, and applied Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate control to pixel-level tests.

The dashboard presents maps, time series, trend estimates, uncertainty, and data availability, making the findings easier to explore and interpret.

Main findings

The available nighttime surface-temperature observations showed a supported increase of approximately 1.09°C per decade, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.89–1.29°C per decade. The full-period daytime trend was statistically inconclusive, while the matched day–night difference decreased by approximately 1.10°C per decade.

These findings describe the analyzed satellite observations. They do not establish the causes of change. We explicitly acknowledge that changes in Terra’s observation time may influence the estimated trends and that land surface temperature differs from air temperature.

Tools and development

We developed the analysis using Python in Google Colab, combining scientific data processing, statistical modeling, and geospatial visualization. We obtained the satellite data through NASA Earthdata Search and exported results for the web dashboard. The project is software-based and does not require custom hardware. Its analytical methods are statistical; we did not train an AI or Machine Learning forecasting model.

Creativity and intended impact

ALDANA connects a long satellite record with a Bahrain-focused, accessible interface inspired by Bahraini identity. Its value lies in presenting temperature patterns alongside evidence strength, missing-data information, and limitations, rather than displaying warming maps alone.

The project can help students develop satellite-data literacy and help researchers identify locations for further investigation and field measurements. It supports the aims of Quality Education, Sustainable Cities and Communities, and Climate Action.

Throughout development, we considered spatial resolution, coastal pixels, cloud-related gaps, seasonal variation, temporal dependence, multiple testing, and satellite observation-time changes. These considerations help users understand both what the evidence shows and what requires further study.
